asr.full_text: I gotta share this with you. This is astonishing, that an analyst at Goldman Sachs actually laid this out in plain English and built an insanely strong argument for us to either aggressively regulate the pharmaceutical industry or even move most community now because of the restrictions. It's almost impossible for any institution to regulate the pharmaceutical industry or even move most pharmaceutical research out of the hands of private for-profit corporations and into government funded students like universities, which by the way, universities and national institutes of health and mental health have funded the majority of new drug research over the decades so it's not like this is something new but but there has been such a move to privatize this stuff such a move an aggressive move to to take the money out of public funding in fact Donald Trump cut public funding into research he cut research he cut research funds on pharmaceuticals well not just Donald just Donald Trump. I mean, you know, it's I doubt he even knew what was going on. Paul Ryan and Mitch McConnell and the entire Republican Party, with this budget that passed without a single Democratic vote, they cut funding for, like, research into … So anyhow, here's what this this analyst says. It's a report for Goldman Sachs titled The Genome Revolution, and he says, "... the potential to deliver one-shot cures is one of the most attractive aspects of gene therapy, genetically engineered cell therapy and gene editing. However, such treatments offer a very different outlook with regard to recurring revenue versus chronic therapies." He says, while this proposition carries tremendous value for patients in societies, it would represent a challenge for genome medicine developers looking for a sustained cash flow. You get this? In other words, he cites the example of a company called Gilead Sciences, which makes a drug that cures Hep C, 90% cure rate with this drug, Hervoni. What happened was, the first year that they rolled this drug out, they had sales of $12.5 billion. Now, I doubt it costs them anything close to that to develop this drug. So that it was massively profitable. But now, they're whining and complaining. That was 2015. That in 2017, the estimate for U.S. sales for 2018 is only going to be $4 billion. Why? Because most people with Hep C have been cured. So now it's not as profitable. There aren't as many potential customers out there. He writes that Guild is a case in point, that's the company that manufactures this drug, where the success of its Hep C franchise has gradually exhausted the available pool of treatable patients. In the case of infectious diseases such as Hepatitis C, curing existing patients also decreases the number of carriers able to transmit the virus to new partners, and thus the incident pool also declines. When an incident pool remains stable, the potential for a cure poses less risk to the sustainability of a franchise, of the company selling the drug. In other words, we don't want to cure people, we just want to keep them taking the drug for the rest of their lives. So now we know the direction that the pharmaceutical industry wants to go when it comes to pharmaceutical research. Hey, letís not actually cure any diseases. Letís try to come up with pills. You see this with the SSRI drugs. You see this with the benzos before them. These are the mental health drugs. You see this with the benzos before them. These are the mental health drugs. You see this with physical health drugs. Let's just, you know, either jack up the price that's gonna prevent them from dying like Heather Bresch did with, you know, Joe Manchin's daughter did, with EpiPen. Or Martin Shirely did with numerous drugs. Let's either jack up the price, and well, Harvoni is 80,000 bucks, or let's only come up with drugs that don't cure people but just kind of keep them on the edge. You're listening to the Tom Hartman program call 202-808-9925. Because then there's more profit especially if they can spread the disease to other people and increase the franchise.
